Value gradients → control
// § 01

SuperMimic as an instance of model-based RL

Model-free methods such as PPO are widely used for robot locomotion and humanoid motion tracking. They learn policies from sampled experience and rewards without learning a dynamics model.

SuperMimic trains a motion-tracking policy by differentiating predicted return through a learned dynamics model. Its reported training efficiency has drawn attention back to model-based RL for humanoid control.

SuperMimic's efficiency comes from applying the established SVG/Dreamer pathwise estimator in a humanoid control loop that keeps its gradients stable.

Model learning and planning

Model-based RL alternates two steps:

  1. Learning: fit a dynamics model to collected transitions, and learn a reward model if the reward is not already known.
  2. Planning: use the model to optimize a policy, or search for an action sequence online and replan at each control step, as in model-predictive control (MPC).

The updated policy or plan supplies transitions for the next round of model learning.

Model-based algorithms

BPTT through 32-step rollouts with a terminal critic

SuperMimic fits a neural dynamics model to transitions from a physics simulator and trains its policy by backpropagation through time (BPTT) over short model rollouts. Let ω\omegaω and ψ\psiψ denote the model and critic parameters.

Let fωf_\omegafω​ be the learned dynamics model. With noise and task conditioning left out of the notation,

at=πθ(s^t),s^t+1=fω(s^t,at).a_t=\pi_\theta(\hat s_t),\qquad \hat s_{t+1}=f_\omega(\hat s_t,a_t).at​=πθ​(s^t​),s^t+1​=fω​(s^t​,at​).

The policy, also called the actor, maximizes rewards over HHH predicted steps plus a critic's estimate of the remaining return:

J^H(θ)=E ⁣[∑t=0H−1γtr(s^t,at)+γHVψ(s^H)].\hat J_H(\theta)=\mathbb E\!\left[ \sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t r(\hat s_t,a_t) +\gamma^H V_\psi(\hat s_H) \right].J^H​(θ)=E[t=0∑H−1​γtr(s^t​,at​)+γHVψ​(s^H​)].

Backpropagation through time (BPTT) differentiates this return with respect to θ\thetaθ through every predicted transition and policy decision.

During the actor update, the model and critic weights stay fixed while gradients pass through their inputs. SuperMimic's reported setup fits the model over eight predicted steps and updates the actor through 32-step rollouts.

In gradient-ascent notation, the actor update is

θ←θ+α∇θJ^H(θ).\theta\leftarrow\theta+\alpha\nabla_\theta\hat J_H(\theta).θ←θ+α∇θ​J^H​(θ).

SuperMimic uses survival weights for termination, omitted here. It fits the model over eight steps and differentiates 32-step actor rollouts.

SuperMimic and the original Dreamer both differentiate predicted return through a learned model and critic. SuperMimic uses a deterministic robot-state model and a terminal critic; Dreamer uses stochastic latent dynamics and critic estimates at every step. Section 2 connects this update to SVG.

// § 02

Policy gradients: pathwise and score-function estimators

PILCO, Dreamer and SuperMimic optimize policies by gradient ascent on expected return. Two common policy-gradient estimators are the score-function estimator and the pathwise estimator.

For an action sampled from πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​, consider L(θ)=E[g(a)]L(\theta)=\mathbb E[g(a)]L(θ)=E[g(a)], where ggg describes its outcome.

  • The score-function estimator, also called the likelihood-ratio or REINFORCE estimator, weights sampled outcomes by the derivative of their log probability:

    ∇θL=E ⁣[(g(a)−b)∇θlog⁡πθ(a)].\nabla_\theta L=\mathbb E\!\left[(g(a)-b)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a)\right].∇θ​L=E[(g(a)−b)∇θ​logπθ​(a)].

    Here bbb is an action-independent baseline. The estimator needs sampled outcomes, but no derivative of ggg.

  • The pathwise estimator writes a=πθ(ϵ)a=\pi_\theta(\epsilon)a=πθ​(ϵ) for parameter-independent noise ϵ\epsilonϵ and differentiates the outcome:

    ∇θL=E ⁣[Dθπθ(ϵ)⊤∇ag(a)].\nabla_\theta L=\mathbb E\!\left[D_\theta\pi_\theta(\epsilon)^\top\nabla_a g(a)\right].∇θ​L=E[Dθ​πθ​(ϵ)⊤∇a​g(a)].

For the same distribution and objective, both estimators give the same gradient under the usual regularity conditions. Adding action noise changes the rollout objective.

In PPO, the score-function estimate weights each sampled action by its estimated advantage:

g^=E^t ⁣[∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)A^t].\hat g=\hat{\mathbb E}_t\!\left[ \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\hat A_t \right].g^​=E^t​[∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)A^t​].

The empirical average is over sampled timesteps, and A^t\hat A_tA^t​ estimates how much better the action was than the critic expected. PPO applies a clipped probability-ratio objective during optimization; its gradient estimate is still score-function based.

Gradient estimators in variational inference

Both estimators have been studied extensively in variational inference, where training a VAE or another latent-variable model requires the gradient of an expectation over sampled latent variables (Kingma and Welling; Rezende et al.). Stochastic computation graphs describe both in a common framework, and Mohamed et al. review their tradeoffs. Two conclusions are well established:

  • Score-function: unbiased and general. It needs only sampled outcomes, so it applies to discrete variables and non-differentiable outcomes, but its variance is high and grows with dimension. In practice it relies on baselines and other control variates.
  • Pathwise: requires a differentiable outcome and a reparameterizable distribution, such as a Gaussian latent. For smooth outcomes it usually has much lower variance, which made reparameterization the standard way to train VAEs.
A variance example

Let a=μ+σϵa=\mu+\sigma\epsilona=μ+σϵ, with ϵ∼N(0,Id)\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)ϵ∼N(0,Id​), and let g(a)=w⊤ag(a)=w^\top ag(a)=w⊤a. The gradient with respect to μ\muμ is www. The pathwise estimator returns exactly www for every sample. The score-function estimator with a scalar baseline bbb has total variance

tr⁡Cov⁡ ⁣[(g(a)−b)∇μlog⁡π(a)]=(d+1)∥w∥2+d(w⊤μ−b)2σ2.\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[(g(a)-b)\nabla_\mu\log\pi(a)\right]=(d+1)\|w\|^2+\frac{d(w^\top\mu-b)^2}{\sigma^2}.trCov[(g(a)−b)∇μ​logπ(a)]=(d+1)∥w∥2+σ2d(w⊤μ−b)2​.

Even with b=w⊤μb=w^\top\mub=w⊤μ, this variance grows with action dimension. The example shows how derivatives can help in a high-dimensional action space, though the variance ordering need not hold for nonlinear dynamics.

Contact, chaos and gradient stability

Chaotic dynamics and stiff contact can make their variance much larger than that of score-function estimates (Parmas et al.; Metz et al.; Suh et al.). Discontinuities can also introduce bias. These are counterexamples to treating the success of reparameterization in variational inference as a general rule for control.

Chaos amplifies sensitivity along a trajectory. For closed-loop Jacobians

At=Dsfω+DafωDsπθ,A_t=D_s f_\omega+D_a f_\omega D_s\pi_\theta,At​=Ds​fω​+Da​fω​Ds​πθ​,

the sensitivity of the final predicted state to the first action is

∂s^H∂a0=AH−1AH−2⋯A1Dafω(s^0,a0).\frac{\partial\hat s_H}{\partial a_0}=A_{H-1}A_{H-2}\cdots A_1 D_a f_\omega(\hat s_0,a_0).∂a0​∂s^H​​=AH−1​AH−2​⋯A1​Da​fω​(s^0​,a0​).

Here DxD_xDx​ denotes a Jacobian. In a chaotic regime, small differences between sampled trajectories can grow through this product, producing large gradients that point in very different directions. The expected return can still be smooth. PIPPS (Parmas et al.) demonstrates this variance problem in model-based policy search and combines pathwise and likelihood-ratio estimates. Metz et al. show exponential growth of gradient variance with rollout length in differentiable control examples. Score-function estimators avoid differentiating through the Jacobian product, though their variance can remain high for other reasons.

Contact introduces both stiffness and discontinuities. A stiff contact model can have large derivatives even when it is continuous. Suh et al. give contact examples where increasing stiffness makes the pathwise estimate noisier than a zeroth-order estimate. At a true discontinuity, differentiating each sampled trajectory can also miss how a policy change moves the boundary between contact outcomes, biasing the estimate. Low empirical variance alone does not establish that the gradient is accurate.

Stability in humanoid control

The humanoid's PD control loop keeps the pathwise gradient stable (Section 3). A learned model smooths contact and supplies derivatives, short rollouts limit prediction error and cost, and a terminal critic estimates the remaining return.

Connection to stochastic value gradients

SuperMimic's actor update follows the value-gradient construction developed in SVG. SVG(0) differentiates an action-value critic; SVG(1) differentiates one model step and a state-value critic; SVG(∞\infty∞) propagates derivatives through a whole trajectory. A finite-horizon version stops the backward pass at a terminal critic, as in SuperMimic.

For one deterministic model step, the action value is Q^1(s,a)=r(s,a)+γVψ(fω(s,a))\widehat Q_1(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma V_\psi(f_\omega(s,a))Q​1​(s,a)=r(s,a)+γVψ​(fω​(s,a)). Its derivative is

∇aQ^1=∇ar+γDafω⊤∇s′Vψ,s′=fω(s,a).\nabla_a\widehat Q_1 =\nabla_a r+\gamma D_a f_\omega^\top\nabla_{s'}V_\psi, \qquad s'=f_\omega(s,a).∇a​Q​1​=∇a​r+γDa​fω⊤​∇s′​Vψ​,s′=fω​(s,a).

An action change affects immediate reward and the next state. The model's Jacobian maps the action change to a state change; the critic's derivative gives its effect on future return. Repeating the chain rule through later policy decisions gives the multistep update.

Original SVG evaluates derivatives along observed transitions and infers the noise that produced them. SuperMimic evaluates them along imagined model trajectories. SHAC also combines a short backward pass with a terminal critic, using a differentiable simulator where SuperMimic uses a learned model.

SuperMimic applies this established update to scalable humanoid tracking and deployment. The derivation starts with SVG(0) and extends it through a full trajectory.

SVG(0), SVG(1), full-trajectory gradients, and related methods

Write the policy's action as a=πθ(s,ϵ)a=\pi_\theta(s,\epsilon)a=πθ​(s,ϵ), with noise independent of θ\thetaθ. At a fixed state, the actor's critic-based objective is

JQ(θ;s)=Eϵ[Qϕ(s,πθ(s,ϵ))],∇θJQ(θ;s)=Eϵ ⁣[Dθπθ(s,ϵ)⊤∇aQϕ(s,a)].\begin{aligned} J_Q(\theta;s)&=\mathbb E_\epsilon[Q_\phi(s,\pi_\theta(s,\epsilon))],\\ \nabla_\theta J_Q(\theta;s) &=\mathbb E_\epsilon\!\left[ D_\theta\pi_\theta(s,\epsilon)^\top\nabla_a Q_\phi(s,a) \right]. \end{aligned}JQ​(θ;s)∇θ​JQ​(θ;s)​=Eϵ​[Qϕ​(s,πθ​(s,ϵ))],=Eϵ​[Dθ​πθ​(s,ϵ)⊤∇a​Qϕ​(s,a)].​

Here DxfD_x fDx​f is the Jacobian of fff with respect to xxx. With the critic weights fixed, its action derivative and the policy Jacobian give the parameter update. This is the update in SVG(0). The zero means no dynamics steps are differentiated before reaching the critic. QϕQ_\phiQϕ​ still estimates future return.

We can instead build the action value from one predicted transition and a state-value critic, holding both networks fixed:

s′=fω(s,a,ξ),Q^1(s,a)=r(s,a)+γEξ[Vψ(s′)],∇aQ^1(s,a)=∇ar(s,a)+γEξ ⁣[Dafω(s,a,ξ)⊤∇s′Vψ(s′)].\begin{aligned} s'&=f_\omega(s,a,\xi),\\ \widehat Q_1(s,a)&=r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb E_\xi[V_\psi(s')],\\ \nabla_a\widehat Q_1(s,a) &=\nabla_a r(s,a) +\gamma\mathbb E_\xi\!\left[D_a f_\omega(s,a,\xi)^\top\nabla_{s'}V_\psi(s')\right]. \end{aligned}s′Q​1​(s,a)∇a​Q​1​(s,a)​=fω​(s,a,ξ),=r(s,a)+γEξ​[Vψ​(s′)],=∇a​r(s,a)+γEξ​[Da​fω​(s,a,ξ)⊤∇s′​Vψ​(s′)].​

Substituting this derivative into the actor update gives

J1(θ;s)=Eϵ[Q^1(s,πθ(s,ϵ))],∇θJ1(θ;s)=Eϵ,ξ ⁣[Dθπθ⊤(∇ar+γDafω⊤∇s′Vψ)].\begin{aligned} J_1(\theta;s)&=\mathbb E_\epsilon[\widehat Q_1(s,\pi_\theta(s,\epsilon))],\\ \nabla_\theta J_1(\theta;s) &=\mathbb E_{\epsilon,\xi}\!\Big[ D_\theta\pi_\theta^\top \big(\nabla_a r+\gamma D_a f_\omega^\top\nabla_{s'}V_\psi\big) \Big]. \end{aligned}J1​(θ;s)∇θ​J1​(θ;s)​=Eϵ​[Q​1​(s,πθ​(s,ϵ))],=Eϵ,ξ​[Dθ​πθ⊤​(∇a​r+γDa​fω⊤​∇s′​Vψ​)].​

This is the one-step gradient underlying SVG(1). The model predicts how an action change affects the next state, and the critic estimates its effect on future return. SVG(0) learns that combined action sensitivity directly through QϕQ_\phiQϕ​. SVG(1) computes it through fωf_\omegafω​ and VψV_\psiVψ​. Both can use a stochastic actor.

For longer rollouts, we apply the chain rule through subsequent actions. For a sampled trajectory, let vsv_svs​ and vθv_\thetavθ​ be the gradients of the remaining discounted return with respect to the current state and policy parameters. A prime denotes the next timestep: vs′′v'_{s'}vs′′​ is the state gradient at s′s's′, and vθ′v'_\thetavθ′​ is the continuation's policy-parameter gradient with s′s's′ held fixed. Holding the sampled noise fixed, backpropagation gives

vθ=(Dθπθ)⊤(∇ar+γ(Dafω)⊤vs′′)+γvθ′,vs=∇sr+(Dsπθ)⊤∇ar+γ(Dsfω+DafωDsπθ)⊤vs′′.\begin{aligned} v_\theta &=(D_\theta\pi_\theta)^\top \left(\nabla_a r+\gamma(D_a f_\omega)^\top v'_{s'}\right) +\gamma v'_\theta,\\[6pt] v_s &=\nabla_s r+(D_s\pi_\theta)^\top\nabla_a r\\ &\quad+\gamma\left(D_s f_\omega+D_a f_\omega D_s\pi_\theta\right)^\top v'_{s'}. \end{aligned}vθ​vs​​=(Dθ​πθ​)⊤(∇a​r+γ(Da​fω​)⊤vs′′​)+γvθ′​,=∇s​r+(Ds​πθ​)⊤∇a​r+γ(Ds​fω​+Da​fω​Ds​πθ​)⊤vs′′​.​

The first equation includes the effect of changing the current action and the policy's later decisions. The second propagates the return gradient through the state and its effect on the policy.

Applying these recursions backward through the full trajectory gives SVG(∞\infty∞). For a finite episode, both continuation gradients start at zero at the terminal boundary. The original SVG(1) and SVG(∞\infty∞) algorithms evaluate learned model derivatives along observed transitions, inferring the noise that produced them. SVG(1) replaces vs′′v'_{s'}vs′′​ with the critic derivative ∇s′Vψ(s′)\nabla_{s'}V_\psi(s')∇s′​Vψ​(s′) and stops the explicit recursion through later policy decisions. Its replay variant also weights the update by the current-to-behavior action-probability ratio.

For an HHH-step look-ahead, we can stop at the predicted state s^H\hat s_Hs^H​ and initialize the backward pass with a terminal critic:

vs=∇sVψ(s)∣s=s^H,vθ=0.v_s=\left.\nabla_sV_\psi(s)\right|_{s=\hat s_H}, \qquad v_\theta=0.vs​=∇s​Vψ​(s)∣s=s^H​​,vθ​=0.

With critic weights fixed, this backward pass gives the short-rollout actor objective in Section 1. SHAC uses this form with a differentiable physics simulator and trains its critic with TD-λ\lambdaλ. SuperMimic uses a learned dynamics model for the rollout and its derivatives. AHAC adapts the horizon to avoid unreliable gradients from stiff dynamics, such as contact. The original Dreamer uses learned latent dynamics and differentiates a λ\lambdaλ-weighted mixture of bootstrapped returns.

A model can also supply training transitions:

s~′=fω(s,a,ξ),D~={(s,a,r(s,a),s~′)}.\tilde s'=f_\omega(s,a,\xi),\qquad \tilde{\mathcal D}=\{(s,a,r(s,a),\tilde s')\}.s~′=fω​(s,a,ξ),D~={(s,a,r(s,a),s~′)}.

MBPO mixes these short synthetic rollouts with real data to train a SAC agent. The actor differentiates its critic and entropy objective; the model supplies data, without appearing in the actor's gradient computation.

At control time, we can search for actions directly. In a learned latent state xtx_txt​, the objective can take the form

a∗(x0)≈arg⁡max⁡a0,…,aH  [∑t=0H−1γtr^(xt,at)+γHQϕ(xH,aH)],xt+1=fω(xt,at).\begin{aligned} \mathbf a^*(x_0)&\approx\underset{a_0,\ldots,a_H}{\arg\max}\; \left[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t\hat r(x_t,a_t) +\gamma^H Q_\phi(x_H,a_H)\right],\\ x_{t+1}&=f_\omega(x_t,a_t). \end{aligned}a∗(x0​)xt+1​​≈a0​,…,aH​argmax​[t=0∑H−1​γtr^(xt​,at​)+γHQϕ​(xH​,aH​)],=fω​(xt​,at​).​

TD-MPC searches this objective by sampling action sequences, executes the first action, and replans. It also learns a policy by differentiating Qϕ(x,πθ(x))Q_\phi(x,\pi_\theta(x))Qϕ​(x,πθ​(x)) with the latent state held fixed. That policy proposes candidate trajectories and supplies actions for critic targets. Planning searches over actions, while the critic gradient updates the policy parameters.

// § 03

Why the same update works now

SuperMimic uses the value-gradient estimator of Heess et al. (2015) and Dreamer v1, differentiating return through a learned model for H steps and bootstrapping with a critic. Dreamer v1 applied pathwise gradients to dm_control; later Dreamers moved away from them. SuperMimic's large gains over PPO on humanoid tracking come from a control loop that keeps this gradient stable.

At horizon H, the gradient contains a product of H closed-loop Jacobians, At = Ds f + Da f · Ds π. Whether that product stays bounded depends on the decision step, actuation, and time spanned by the horizon. SuperMimic's humanoid receives PD position targets at 50 Hz: H = 32 spans 0.64 s, and the servo contracts errors at every step. Dreamer's dm_control robot receives direct torque held for 50 ms: H = 32 spans 1.6 s, with nothing in the plant pulling errors back.

We compared gradients on G1 (20 ms PD targets) and the dm_control walker and humanoid (50 ms torque), keeping the update, networks, clipping and training recipe fixed.

Closed-loop values at 32 steps are 90th percentiles over start states; open loop removes the policy's feedback.

Table 4. The gradient the two loops return.
LoopGradient normSignal gain (×)Saturation (%)
G11 to 821 to 36-
Torque103 to 105-100

H = 32. Torque norms are run medians; signal gain is the pathwise SNR over the score-function SNR; saturation is the share of actor tanh outputs at ±1.

On G1, policy feedback through the PD loop contracts the Jacobians, keeping the gradient norm between 1 and 8 throughout training. The signal-to-noise advantage holds on the same rollouts at every horizon from 1 to 128. On dm_control, the closed-loop product is 102 to 108 times the open-loop product: feedback through direct torque amplifies errors. Gradient medians reach 103 to 105 within 100k frames, with spikes to 1011; all actor outputs saturate by 600k frames.

Two controls locate the cause. Halving the dm_control humanoid's decision step to 25 ms, so H = 32 spans 0.8 s, lowers the median from 105 to between 2 and 93 at the same number of actor updates; lengthening the Isaac humanoid's step to 50 ms, so H = 32 spans 1.6 s, raises its gradient about tenfold, and it stays bounded. The span sets the size of the gradient; the loop decides whether the product stays bounded, and at 0.8 s the dm_control humanoid still spikes to 106 to 107 and does not learn. Switching between SuperMimic's clipping (norm 1, then 0.1 per element) and Dreamer's (norm 100) changes nothing in either setting.

On G1, the update reaches PPO's 4-hour tracking quality in about 1.3 hours. On walker-walk, it scores 19 to 68 out of 1,000 at Dreamer's full 5M-frame budget under either clipping rule; Dreamer v1 scores 956 at 1M frames. Dreamer v1 learns walker-walk with its own latent model, H = 15 and tuning; the same update through a state model in that loop does not.

Modern humanoid environments supply SuperMimic's stable gradient through 50 Hz PD position control. The robotics community built this loop for PPO; SuperMimic uses it with rollout horizons under a second. SVG(H) and SHAC use the same pathwise construction. SuperMimic's learned model supplies the derivatives without a differentiable simulator. The estimator dates to 2015.

// § 04

Sources of efficiency

In the stable control loop of Section 3, the pathwise estimator reduces gradient noise, the model supplies fast rollouts and derivatives, and the terminal critic supports short horizons.

Pathwise gradients have higher signal-to-noise ratio

At three LAFAN1 checkpoints, we froze the policy, model and critic and measured gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) from 64 independent minibatches of 4,096 imagined rollouts:

SNR=∥E[g^]∥tr⁡Cov⁡[g^].\mathrm{SNR}=\frac{\|\mathbb E[\hat g]\|}{\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}[\hat g]}}.SNR=trCov[g^​]​∥E[g^​]∥​.

Both estimators use Gaussian action noise with standard deviation 0.1. The pathwise estimate differentiates the reparameterized rollout; the score-function estimate uses the checkpoint critic and standardized per-step advantages.

At H=32H=32H=32, the pathwise SNR is 27–34 times higher across the three checkpoints (Figure 3): the gradient varies less relative to its mean.

Probe values and interpretation
CheckpointReparameterized pathwise SNRScore-function SNRRatio
0.5 h8.710.2633.5
1.5 h12.430.4130.3
4 h8.310.3126.8

The deterministic pathwise update has SNR 8.83, 12.64 and 9.32 at these checkpoints. The reparameterized comparison matches action noise to keep the rollout objective the same.

With 64 draws, a near-zero mean gradient produces an estimated SNR on the order of 1/64=0.1251/\sqrt{64}=0.1251/64​=0.125 from sampling noise alone.

The update uses fewer imagined steps than PPO

The SuperMimic paper, Figure 5(b), compares its actor–critic update with PPO trained on world-model rollouts. On LAFAN1 walk/run/sprint motions, it reports reaching PPO-WM's best training return with about 64 times fewer imagined steps. Both methods have access to model rollouts, so this comparison supports a contribution from the policy update beyond rollout throughput.

The critic supports short rollouts

We compared training with a terminal critic against training without any value function at H=8H=8H=8 and H=32H=32H=32 (Figure 4).

At H=8H=8H=8, removing the value function increases local tracking error from 21.5 to 40.8 mm and reduces success from 92.3% to 28.6%. At H=32H=32H=32, local error changes less, from 24.4 to 25.1 mm, but global error increases from 226 to 468 mm. The critic still helps global tracking at the longer horizon, even though its effect on local pose error is small.

Local error measures root-relative positions of 14 tracked bodies; global error uses world coordinates. Success means reaching the episode limit or clip end without a tracking failure. Evaluation uses mean actions on 40 LAFAN1 clips.

The stable gradient drives efficiency

The stable pathwise update learns from fewer imagined steps than PPO. The model supplies derivatives, and the terminal critic extends the return beyond short rollouts.

SuperMimic also reports model rollouts more than ten times faster than its simulator at practical batch sizes.

Deterministic pathwise SNR stays high through H = 128 in this control loop. Shorter rollouts save compute and limit accumulated prediction error.

// § 05

Beyond BPTT: better gradient estimators

The same estimator on recorded data

Imagined BPTT differentiates H-step model predictions, so model error enters every forward value of the gradient: 36 mm at 32 steps and 146 mm at 64 steps on LAFAN1. Heess et al.'s original SVG(H) runs the forward pass on recorded states with the recorded noise inferred and uses the model only for local derivatives. The interactive figure below shows the difference on a one-parameter toy. We trained it on the same humanoid tracker with the same recipe.

On a 29-joint chain built to G1's shape, where the exact pathwise gradient through the true dynamics can be computed, the two estimators' gradients on the replay windows they train on compare as follows.

On LAFAN1, the better gradient estimate yields a better result.

Inspiration from the variational inference literature

REBAR and RELAX: combine both estimators. They keep a score-function term, so the estimate stays unbiased and applies to discrete samples, but apply it only to the residual between the outcome and a differentiable surrogate; pathwise terms through the surrogate supply the rest. For a discrete sample b∼pθb\sim p_\thetab∼pθ​, let g(b)g(b)g(b) be its outcome and ccc the surrogate. Their shared estimator is

g^θ=[g(b)−c(z~)]∇θlog⁡pθ(b)+∇θc(z)−∇θc(z~).\begin{aligned} \hat g_\theta &=[g(b)-c(\tilde z)]\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(b)\\ &\quad+\nabla_\theta c(z)-\nabla_\theta c(\tilde z). \end{aligned}g^​θ​​=[g(b)−c(z~)]∇θ​logpθ​(b)+∇θ​c(z)−∇θ​c(z~).​

Here zzz is a continuous sample that maps to bbb by a hard threshold or categorical choice; z~\tilde zz~ is drawn from its conditional distribution given that same bbb. Both draws are reparameterized. The last two derivatives follow those draws, holding bbb fixed for the conditional one and holding the surrogate's parameters fixed.

The residual g(b)−c(z~)g(b)-c(\tilde z)g(b)−c(z~) fluctuates much less than the full outcome, so the estimator has low variance while remaining unbiased. REBAR builds ccc from a continuous relaxation of the objective; RELAX learns it to minimize gradient variance.

A residual score-function correction (REBAR’s construction, with the SVG term as control variate) adds nothing on recorded LAFAN1 windows: the model-free score gradient already agrees with the SVG gradient (cosine 0.83 to 0.93, at 0.82 to 0.86 of its size), and the action noise explains about 1% of the advantage variance. Trained online the correction only adds noise, and real residuals do no better than shuffled ones.

Learn the action gradient through a critic

Model-free methods such as deterministic policy gradient (DPG) and TD3 differentiate an action-value critic. It estimates the future return that SuperMimic computes through a model rollout.

For a deterministic actor a=μθ(s)a=\mu_\theta(s)a=μθ​(s), the gradient at a sampled state is

g^θ=Dθμθ(s)⊤∇aQϕ(s,a)∣a=μθ(s).\hat g_\theta =D_\theta\mu_\theta(s)^\top \left.\nabla_a Q_\phi(s,a)\right|_{a=\mu_\theta(s)}.g^​θ​=Dθ​μθ​(s)⊤∇a​Qϕ​(s,a)∣a=μθ​(s)​.

The critic's action derivative gives the effect on future return; the policy Jacobian converts it into a parameter update.

The actor's differentiation horizon and the critic's target horizon are separate. Multistep returns and model-based value expansion train the critic with more rewards while keeping the same actor update.

DPG and TD3, model-based value expansion, and multistep critic targets

Consider a deterministic policy a=μθ(s)a=\mu_\theta(s)a=μθ​(s) and an action-value critic Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s,a)Qϕ​(s,a) trained from a replay buffer D\mathcal DD. With the critic weights held fixed, the actor maximizes the estimated return of its actions at sampled states:

JQ(θ)=Es∼D[Qϕ(s,μθ(s))],∇θJQ=Es∼D ⁣[Dθμθ(s)⊤∇aQϕ(s,a)∣a=μθ(s)].\begin{aligned} J_Q(\theta)&=\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D}[Q_\phi(s,\mu_\theta(s))],\\ \nabla_\theta J_Q &=\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D}\!\left[ D_\theta\mu_\theta(s)^\top \nabla_a Q_\phi(s,a)\big|_{a=\mu_\theta(s)} \right]. \end{aligned}JQ​(θ)∇θ​JQ​​=Es∼D​[Qϕ​(s,μθ​(s))],=Es∼D​[Dθ​μθ​(s)⊤∇a​Qϕ​(s,a)​a=μθ​(s)​].​

This is the deterministic policy gradient (DPG) used by TD3. It is the deterministic-actor counterpart of SVG(0). “Deterministic” describes the actor: QQQ still estimates expected future return, including any randomness in the environment. SVG(1) computes the action derivative through one model step and a state-value critic.

A critic trained with one-step TD targets still estimates the full discounted return.

Train the critic on rollout returns

Differentiating a model rollout's rewards and terminal value gives SVG with a deterministic policy.

Fix a continuation policy μˉ\bar\muμˉ​ and terminal critic VψV_\psiVψ​. Write the HHH-step return as a function of its first action:

Q^Hμˉ(s,a)=E ⁣[∑t=0H−1γtr(s^t,at)+γHVψ(s^H)  |  s^0=s, a0=a].\hat Q_H^{\bar\mu}(s,a)=\mathbb E\!\left[ \sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t r(\hat s_t,a_t) +\gamma^H V_\psi(\hat s_H) \;\middle|\;\hat s_0=s,\ a_0=a \right].Q^​Hμˉ​​(s,a)=E[t=0∑H−1​γtr(s^t​,at​)+γHVψ​(s^H​)​s^0​=s, a0​=a].

After the first action, at=μˉ(s^t)a_t=\bar\mu(\hat s_t)at​=μˉ​(s^t​) for t≥1t\geq1t≥1. We can compute this return by unrolling the model, or train Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s,a)Qϕ​(s,a) to predict it. The actor can then differentiate the critic.

Model-Based Value Expansion (MVE) uses short model rollouts to construct critic targets. Multistep returns from real trajectories provide another source of targets.

Multistep targets and TD3–λ\lambdaλ

An nnn-step critic target takes nnn rewards before using a target critic for the rest:

yt(n)=∑k=0n−1γkrt+k+γnQˉ(st+n,μˉ(st+n)).y_t^{(n)}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma^k r_{t+k} +\gamma^n\bar Q(s_{t+n},\bar\mu(s_{t+n})).yt(n)​=k=0∑n−1​γkrt+k​+γnQˉ​(st+n​,μˉ​(st+n​)).

Bars denote target networks. A truncated λ\lambdaλ-return averages different target lengths:

yt(λ,N)=(1−λ)∑n=1N−1λn−1yt(n)+λN−1yt(N).y_t^{(\lambda,N)}= (1-\lambda)\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\lambda^{n-1}y_t^{(n)} +\lambda^{N-1}y_t^{(N)}.yt(λ,N)​=(1−λ)n=1∑N−1​λn−1yt(n)​+λN−1yt(N)​.

Longer targets rely less on the critic's current estimate, but can have higher variance. Replay trajectories also contain actions from older policies, so the choice of off-policy return matters.

Kozuno et al. (ICML 2021) tested TD3 with one-step targets, nnn-step targets, Peng's Q(λ\lambdaλ), Retrace, and C-trace. Peng's Q(λ\lambdaλ) performed strongly in their continuous-control experiments. D4PG also combines deterministic actor gradients with multistep returns, and FastTD3 supports multistep targets.

BPTT differentiates every policy decision in the rollout; the frozen-critic update differentiates the current action. The deterministic policy-gradient theorem relates action-value derivatives to the full return gradient using the current policy's value function and discounted state distribution. Critic error, finite rollout horizons, and replay sampling affect how closely practical updates match that gradient.

// § 06

Planning, planning, and planning

A dynamics model can support control through samples, derivatives or predictive features. These uses can be combined:

THREE USES OF A DYNAMICS MODEL
01Sample-based planning

PETS and the TD-MPC planner evaluate candidate action sequences through model rollouts. Dyna and MBPO generate transitions for a policy learner.

02Gradient-based planning

PILCO, SVG and SuperMimic differentiate learned dynamics to improve actions or policies; SHAC differentiates a simulator.

03Representation-based planning

Spectral representations extract predictive features from learned transitions for value-function approximation.

Learn predictive features for value estimation

Spectral representation-based RL derives predictive features from the transition operator. The linear factorization below lets us fit the continuation value by linear regression once the features are fixed.

A linear transition factorization gives

p(s′∣s,a)=ϕ(s,a)⊤ν(s′),Qπ(s,a)=r(s,a)+γϕ(s,a)⊤wπ,\begin{aligned} p(s'\mid s,a)&=\phi(s,a)^\top\nu(s'),\\ Q^\pi(s,a)&=r(s,a)+\gamma\phi(s,a)^\top w^\pi, \end{aligned}p(s′∣s,a)Qπ(s,a)​=ϕ(s,a)⊤ν(s′),=r(s,a)+γϕ(s,a)⊤wπ,​

where wπ=∫ν(s′)Vπ(s′) ds′w^\pi=\int\nu(s')V^\pi(s')\,ds'wπ=∫ν(s′)Vπ(s′)ds′. The expected continuation value is a linear function of the predictive features, as in SPEDER.

A latent-variable model writes

p(s′∣s,a)=∫p(z∣s,a)p(s′∣z) dz.p(s'\mid s,a)=\int p(z\mid s,a)p(s'\mid z)\,dz.p(s′∣s,a)=∫p(z∣s,a)p(s′∣z)dz.

LV-Rep uses the conditional distribution p(z∣s,a)p(z\mid s,a)p(z∣s,a) as the predictive representation for value learning.

An energy-based formulation

An energy-based transition model writes

log⁡p(s′∣s,a)=u(s,a)⊤v(s′)−log⁡Z(s,a),\log p(s'\mid s,a)=u(s,a)^\top v(s')-\log Z(s,a),logp(s′∣s,a)=u(s,a)⊤v(s′)−logZ(s,a),

where ZZZ normalizes the density. The inner product measures how well a next state matches the current state and action. Differentiating with respect to the next state removes ZZZ:

∇s′log⁡p(s′∣s,a)=Ds′v(s′)⊤u(s,a).\nabla_{s'}\log p(s'\mid s,a)=D_{s'}v(s')^\top u(s,a).∇s′​logp(s′∣s,a)=Ds′​v(s′)⊤u(s,a).

This derivative is the score. DiffSR learns predictive features with a noise-conditioned score model, then transforms those features for value approximation.

This construction also models transitions between motion windows conditioned on a skill.

Diagram: predicting states and predicting values

Spectral Skills: predicting motion windows

Spectral Skills learns a humanoid whole-body controller that imitates reference motions. Its dynamics model predicts motion windows, whereas SuperMimic models the effect of robot actions on the simulated state.

We factor transitions between motion windows in an offline reference dataset to learn skill commands for a controller. The factorization gives directions for steering and combining motions.

Let xtx_txt​ be the state at frame ttt in a reference motion. For a segment starting at frame TTT, define three ordered windows of states:

X=(xT−P,…,xT−1),B=(xT,…,xT+K−1),Y=(xT+K,…,xT+K+L).\begin{aligned} X&=(x_{T-P},\ldots,x_{T-1}),\\ B&=(x_T,\ldots,x_{T+K-1}),\\ Y&=(x_{T+K},\ldots,x_{T+K+L}). \end{aligned}XBY​=(xT−P​,…,xT−1​),=(xT​,…,xT+K−1​),=(xT+K​,…,xT+K+L​).​

XXX contains the PPP states before frame TTT, BBB contains the next KKK states to encode, and YYY contains the following L+1L+1L+1 states to predict.

The encoder maps BBB to a skill z=E(B)z=E(B)z=E(B). Given XXX and zzz, the dynamics model learns the distribution of YYY.

Learn a motion command we can steer

Prediction trains zzz to capture how a motion continues. We also want to change that motion through zzz, for example by adding a turn to a walk. The factorization below lets us derive the predicted effect of changing the skill.

The energy depends on the skill through an affine map—a linear map plus an offset. With a fixed base measure,

log⁡p(Y∣X,z)=ϕ(X,z)⊤μ(Y)−log⁡Z(X,z),ϕ(X,z)=F(X)⊤(Az+b).\begin{aligned} \log p(Y\mid X,z)&=\phi(X,z)^\top\mu(Y)-\log Z(X,z),\\ \phi(X,z)&=F(X)^\top(Az+b). \end{aligned}logp(Y∣X,z)ϕ(X,z)​=ϕ(X,z)⊤μ(Y)−logZ(X,z),=F(X)⊤(Az+b).​

The diffusion noise predictor preserves this structure:

D(X,z,Yτ,τ)=M(Yτ,τ)⊤F(X)⊤(Az+b).D(X,z,Y^\tau,\tau) =M(Y^\tau,\tau)^\top F(X)^\top(Az+b).D(X,z,Yτ,τ)=M(Yτ,τ)⊤F(X)⊤(Az+b).

Training adds noise, Yτ=ατY+στϵY^\tau=\alpha_\tau Y+\sigma_\tau\epsilonYτ=ατ​Y+στ​ϵ, and fits the encoder and predictor to recover ϵ\epsilonϵ.

Derive the steering response

Fix q=(X,Yτ,τ)q=(X,Y^\tau,\tau)q=(X,Yτ,τ): the context, noisy future, and noise level, with ατ>0\alpha_\tau>0ατ​>0. Write Cq=M(Yτ,τ)⊤F(X)⊤C_q=M(Y^\tau,\tau)^\top F(X)^\topCq​=M(Yτ,τ)⊤F(X)⊤. Substituting the noise predictor into Tweedie's formula gives a single-step clean-motion estimate in normalized coordinates:

Y^q(z)=Yτ−στD(q,z)ατ=cq+Jqz,cq=Yτ−στCqbατ,Jq=−στατCqA.\begin{aligned} \widehat Y_q(z) &=\frac{Y^\tau-\sigma_\tau D(q,z)}{\alpha_\tau}\\ &=c_q+J_qz,\\[4pt] c_q&=\frac{Y^\tau-\sigma_\tau C_qb}{\alpha_\tau},\\ J_q&=-\frac{\sigma_\tau}{\alpha_\tau}C_qA. \end{aligned}Yq​(z)cq​Jq​​=ατ​Yτ−στ​D(q,z)​=cq​+Jq​z,=ατ​Yτ−στ​Cq​b​,=−ατ​στ​​Cq​A.​

Neither cqc_qcq​ nor JqJ_qJq​ depends on zzz. Steering by any offset δ\deltaδ therefore gives

Y^q(z+δ)−Y^q(z)=Jqδ.\widehat Y_q(z+\delta)-\widehat Y_q(z)=J_q\delta.Yq​(z+δ)−Yq​(z)=Jq​δ.

The response matrix JqJ_qJq​ does not change with the starting skill. At a fixed qqq, adding the same offset to two different skills therefore produces the same change in the predicted motion. The relation is exact for finite offsets.

It also gives a direct rule for composition. For offsets δ1,δ2\delta_1,\delta_2δ1​,δ2​ and weights η1,η2\eta_1,\eta_2η1​,η2​,

Y^q(z+η1δ1+η2δ2)−Y^q(z)=η1Jqδ1+η2Jqδ2.\begin{aligned} &\widehat Y_q(z+\eta_1\delta_1+\eta_2\delta_2)-\widehat Y_q(z)\\ &\qquad=\eta_1J_q\delta_1+\eta_2J_q\delta_2. \end{aligned}​Yq​(z+η1​δ1​+η2​δ2​)−Yq​(z)=η1​Jq​δ1​+η2​Jq​δ2​.​

The weighted effects add, so we can reuse and combine directions across base skills. These identities hold for the single-step estimate at fixed qqq; we evaluate the resulting robot behavior through the trained controller.

Find directions, then steer the controller

To find directions with a strong predicted effect across the data, stack the response matrices from sampled queries:

J=1N[Jq1⋮JqN],J=UΣV⊤.\mathcal J=\frac{1}{\sqrt N} \begin{bmatrix}J_{q_1}\\ \vdots\\ J_{q_N}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathcal J=U\Sigma V^\top.J=N​1​​Jq1​​⋮JqN​​​​,J=UΣV⊤.

The columns viv_ivi​ of VVV are the steering directions. The squared singular value σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​ measures each direction's average squared predicted effect:

1N∑j=1N∥Jqjvi∥2=σi2.\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|J_{q_j}v_i\|^2=\sigma_i^2.N1​j=1∑N​∥Jqj​​vi​∥2=σi2​.

We then freeze the encoder and train a low-level policy πlo(a∣o,z)\pi^{\mathrm{lo}}(a\mid o,z)πlo(a∣o,z) with PPO to imitate the reference motions. The controller converts the skill command into robot actions. We test the steering directions through this controller to identify effects such as arm raising or turning.

For a walking reference, we encode successive motion windows to obtain a sequence of base commands ztbasez_t^{\mathrm{base}}ztbase​. At each control step, steering adds weighted directions:

ztsteer=ztbase+∑iηi(t) vi.z_t^{\mathrm{steer}}=z_t^{\mathrm{base}}+\sum_i\eta_i(t)\,v_i.ztsteer​=ztbase​+i∑​ηi​(t)vi​.

Each coefficient ηi(t)\eta_i(t)ηi​(t) controls a direction's sign and strength over time. Adding arm and turn directions to the walk asks the robot to walk with its arm raised while turning. The frozen controller receives the combined command and the current observation:

at∼πlo(⋅∣ot,ztsteer).a_t\sim\pi^{\mathrm{lo}}(\cdot\mid o_t,z_t^{\mathrm{steer}}).at​∼πlo(⋅∣ot​,ztsteer​).

Combining the two levels

A SuperMimic-style BPTT update could train the Spectral Skills controller with an action-conditioned robot dynamics model alongside the motion predictor.

See the Spectral Skills project page for steering and composition demos, and the SuperMimic project page for model-based policy training.
